title: Plane Polarization of Light
short_intro: Plane polarization is the restriction of the vibration of the electric field vector of a light wave to a single plane containing the direction of propagation. It provides unequivocal proof of the transverse nature of light waves.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of transverse waves, polarization by reflection (Brewster's law), polarization by refraction, and polaroids.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative treatment of Malus's law, double refraction in uniaxial crystals (ordinary and extraordinary rays), Nicole prism, quarter-wave and half-wave plates, and optical activity.

prerequisites: Maxwell's electromagnetic wave equations (electric and magnetic field vectors)
Snell's law of refraction and total internal reflection

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Unpolarized and Polarized Light
bullets: Unpolarized light consists of electromagnetic waves with rapidly and randomly changing planes of electric field vibration perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Plane-polarized (or linearly polarized) light confines its electric field vector E to a fixed plane throughout its propagation.
The intensity of unpolarized light is equally distributed in all azimuths perpendicular to the wave normal.

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection and Brewster's Law
bullets: When unpolarized light is incident at a specific angle called the polarizing angle (or Brewster's angle, i<sub>p</sub>) on a transparent medium, the reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and the refracted ray are mutually perpendicular to each other.
Brewster's law states that the tangent of the polarizing angle is numerically equal to the refractive index of the medium (μ = tan i<sub>p</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Double Refraction and Birefringence
bullets: Certain crystals like calcite and quartz split an unpolarized incident ray into two refracted rays: the Ordinary ray (O-ray) and the Extraordinary ray (E-ray).
The O-ray obeys ordinary laws of refraction and travels with the same speed in all directions within the crystal.
The E-ray does not obey Snell's law, travels with varying speeds depending on the direction, and its refractive index varies with the angle of incidence.

concept_notes.heading: Optical Activity and Specific Rotation
bullets: Optically active substances (e.g., quartz, sugar solution, turpentine) rotate the plane of polarization of linearly polarized light passing through them.
The angle of rotation θ is directly proportional to the length of the path (l) and the concentration (c) of the solution.
Specific rotation is defined as the rotation produced by a solution of length 1 decimetre and unit concentration (1 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) at a specified temperature for a given wavelength.

derivations.title: Derivation of Brewster's Law
derivations.conditions: Light incident on a dielectric boundary at polarizing angle i<sub>p</sub>
steps: Let unpolarized light be incident at Brewster's angle i<sub>p</sub> such that the reflected ray is completely polarized with electric vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
At this angle, the angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray (angle of refraction r) is exactly 90 degrees.
From the geometry of the interface, the angle of incidence i<sub>p</sub> + 90\deg + r = 180\deg, which gives r = 90\deg - i<sub>p</sub>.
Applying Snell's law at the boundary: \mu = \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin r}.
Substitute r = 90\deg - i<sub>p</sub> into Snell's law: \mu = \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin(90\deg - i_p)} = \frac{\sin i_p}{\cos i_p} = \tan i_p.

derivations.title: Derivation of Malus's Law
derivations.conditions: Plane-polarized light of initial amplitude E<sub>0</sub> incident on an analyzer with transmission axis at angle \theta
steps: Let the electric field vector of the incoming plane-polarized light be E<sub>0</sub>.

When this light passes through an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle \theta with the vibration plane of the incident light, the electric vector is resolved into two orthogonal components.
The component parallel to the transmission axis is E<sub>0</sub> \cos \theta, and the component perpendicular is E<sub>0</sub> \sin \theta.
Only the parallel component is transmitted by the analyzer.
Since intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude (I \propto E<sup>2</sup>), the transmitted intensity I is given by I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta, where I<sub>0</sub> is the initial intensity.

formula_sheet.name: Malus's Law
formula_sheet.variables: I = Transmitted intensity, I_0 = Incident intensity, \theta = Angle between polarizers

formula_sheet.conditions: Introduces a path difference of \lambda/4 or phase difference of \pi/2

formula_sheet.name: Thickness of Half-Wave Plate
formula_sheet.variables: t = Thickness, \lambda = Wavelength, n_e, n_o = Principal refractive indices
formula_sheet.conditions: Introduces a path difference of \lambda/2 or phase difference of \pi

formula_sheet.name: Optical Rotation Angle
formula_sheet.variables: \theta = Angle of rotation, S = Specific rotation, l = Path length, c = Concentration

formula_sheet.name: Average Intensity of Unpolarized Light through Polarizer
formula_sheet.variables: I = Transmitted intensity, I_0 = Unpolarized incident intensity
formula_sheet.conditions: Averaged over all azimuth angles \theta (since average of \cos^2 \theta is 1/2)

formula_sheet.name: Law of Malus for Amplitude
formula_sheet.variables: E = Transmitted electric field amplitude, E_0 = Incident amplitude

graphs_and_experiments.title: Malus's Law Verification Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of transmitted intensity (I) versus \cos^2 \theta (or angle \theta showing a symmetric cosine-squared wave curve between 0 and 360 degrees).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The linear straight-line plot of I versus \cos^2 \theta confirms the direct proportionality predicted by Malus's law.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual MCQs regarding maximum and minimum positions when rotating an analyzer.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization by Reflection (Brewster's Angle setup)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray diagram showing unpolarized light incident on a glass slab at i<sub>p</sub>, with reflected ray completely polarized (perpendicular dots) and refracted ray partially polarized, making a 90-degree angle between them.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the physical condition where reflected and refracted rays are orthogonal at the polarizing angle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly asked in TGT/PGT theoretical questions about the angle between reflected and refracted beams.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nicol Prism Construction and Action
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A calcite crystal cut diagonally and cemented with Canada balsam, showing total internal reflection of the ordinary ray and transmission of the extraordinary ray.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how a single polarizing device isolates a pure extraordinary plane-polarized beam.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Question source for identifying crystal cuts and optical cement (Canada balsam refractive index properties).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the polarizing angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.

Unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m<sup>2</sup> is incident on a polarizer. The transmitted light falls on a second polarizer (analyzer) whose transmission axis is oriented at 60 degrees to the first polarizer. Find the final transmitted intensity.
solution_steps: When unpolarized light passes through the first polarizer, its intensity is reduced to half: I_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times 32 = 16 \text{ W/m}^2.
Apply Malus's law for the second polarizer: I_2 = I_1 \cos^2 \theta

solved_numericals.question: A quarter-wave plate is designed for sodium light of wavelength 589 nm. If the principal refractive indices are n_e = 1.553 and n_o = 1.544, calculate the minimum thickness of the plate.
solution_steps: Use the formula for the thickness of a quarter-wave plate: t = \frac{\lambda}{4(n_e - n_o)}
Substitute the given values: \lambda = 589 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}, n_e = 1.553, n_o = 1.544

assumptions_and_limitations: Ideal polarizers are assumed to have 100% transmission for parallel electric vector components and 0% for perpendicular components (infinite extinction ratio).
Linear optical media are assumed where refractive indices are independent of light intensity.
Birefringent plates assume uniform thickness and homogeneous crystal structure throughout the active aperture.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Longitudinal waves like sound waves can be polarized.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only transverse waves can be polarized.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization requires oscillations to occur perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which is impossible in longitudinal compression waves.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Unpolarized light has no electric field components.
common_misconceptions.correct: Unpolarized light has rapid, randomly fluctuating electric field components in all directions perpendicular to the ray.
common_misconceptions.why: Zero time-average value across all azimuths does not mean the instantaneous field vector is zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The angle between the reflected and refracted rays at any incidence angle is 90 degrees.
common_misconceptions.correct: The reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular only when incidence is at Brewster's polarizing angle.
common_misconceptions.why: Snell's law dictates that r varies with i, and orthogonality is a special geometric consequence unique to i = i_p.

quick_revision: Polarization proves the transverse nature of light waves.
Brewster's Law: \mu = \tan i_p with reflected and refracted rays mutually perpendicular.
Unpolarized light passing through an ideal polarizer drops to exactly half its initial intensity.
Calcite crystal exhibits double refraction producing O-ray and E-ray.
Quarter-wave plate introduces a phase difference of \pi/2; half-wave plate introduces \pi.
